title_original: Week in wildlife: Christmas crabs, a shy possum and baboons taking liberties
excerpt_original: This week’s best wildlife photographs from around the world Continue reading...

blocks.text: Gentoo penguins on the beach at Port Howard, Falkland Islands. The islands host a population of more than 1m penguins during the summer breeding season, but that number may drop this year due to bird flu – a disease that gentoos are particularly susceptible to, since they remain on shore year roundPhotograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

Chacma baboon parents settle down to dinner as their children play on a car in Cape Town, South Africa. Forty-four of the baboons have been captured and relocated to a sanctuary, a move that has pleased some and angered others Photograph: Nic Bothma/Reuters
Great white pelicans at Milleyha wetland, a key stopover for migratory birds on Turkey’s Mediterranean coastPhotograph: Meric Aktar/Anadolu/Getty Images

A Caucasian grouse in Rize, Turkey. Living in high mountains above 2,000 metres, this rare species survives harsh weather conditions during winter, heading to forested areas for shelter and foodPhotograph: Alper Tüydeş/Anadolu/Getty Images

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific. This imagery was captured at a safe distance using red or infrared lighting to protect the turtlesPhotograph: Robin Riggs/Aquarium of the Pacific
A cocoi heron stands in the waters of Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon, contemplating its plastic paddle-boat neighbours, in Rio de Janeiro, BrazilPhotograph: Bob Karp/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
Blue morpho butterflies visit a feeding station near where the Cop31 climate change conference was taking place in Antalya, TurkeyPhotograph: Yasin Akgül/AFP/Getty Images

Red crabs cross a road during their migration on Christmas Island, Australia. Millions of crabs are beginning their annual mass migration toward the island’s beaches, where they must go in order to breedPhotograph: Parks Australia/Reuters
